quiz.question: What does an anonymous pipe transfer between processes?
options: Only discrete, complete application messages
An ordered, unidirectional byte stream without inherent message boundaries
Directly mapped physical memory frames
Signals carrying arbitrary 64-bit user payloads
quiz.explanation: A pipe is a unidirectional byte stream. The kernel manages an ordered stream of bytes; it does not preserve write boundaries. The reading process must define a framing protocol if discrete messages are required.

quiz.question: When does a process reading from a pipe receive EOF (read() returns 0)?
options: Whenever the writing process pauses or sleeps
When the kernel pipe buffer becomes more than 50% full
After all file descriptors referring to the write end have been closed AND buffered data is consumed
Immediately after the child process forks
quiz.explanation: A pipe reader only receives EOF (read returns 0) when every copy of the write-end file descriptor across all processes has been closed and any remaining bytes in the kernel buffer have been read.

quiz.question: Which IPC mechanism is optimal for transferring massive bulk data (such as 4K video frames or ML tensors) between local processes?
options: Signals with sigqueue()
POSIX Shared Memory (shm_open + mmap)
SIGCHLD notifications
A FIFO pathname without an application buffer
quiz.explanation: POSIX Shared Memory allows processes to map identical physical RAM frames into their respective address spaces, eliminating the double-copy overhead of kernel socket or pipe buffers.

quiz.question: Why must a stream-socket (SOCK_STREAM) receiver implement application-level message framing?
options: Stream reads are guaranteed to preserve individual send() boundaries
A single recv() call may return a partial message, a full message, or fragments of multiple messages
Unix domain sockets cannot transfer binary bytes
Framing turns off kernel TCP/IP checksum calculation
quiz.explanation: SOCK_STREAM delivers an arbitrary byte stream. Network or kernel buffers can fragment or coalesce messages; the receiving application must use length prefixes, delimiters, or fixed sizes to reconstruct complete requests.

quiz.question: What is an async-signal-safe strategy for handling SIGINT or SIGTERM to request a graceful shutdown?
options: Call printf() and malloc() repeatedly inside the signal handler
Invoke waitpid() in a blocking loop inside the handler
Set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag in the handler and handle cleanup in the main event loop
Close all database connections and flush disk buffers directly inside the signal handler
quiz.explanation: Signal handlers interrupt arbitrary execution and can cause deadlocks if they invoke non-reentrant functions (like printf or malloc). Setting a volatile sig_atomic_t flag allows the normal program loop to safely initiate cleanup.

quiz.question: What is backpressure in an IPC architecture?
options: An unbounded queue that grows infinitely to avoid slowing the producer
A flow-control mechanism that throttles or blocks fast producers when slow consumers cannot keep up
A specific Unix signal sent when disk space is exhausted
A kernel method that terminates processes with broken pipes
quiz.explanation: Backpressure prevents fast producers from overwhelming slow consumers. By capping queue capacity and blocking writers (or returning 429/busy errors), it prevents memory exhaustion and unconstrained latency spikes.
